name: Apple
notes: Crisp, sweet-tart flavour. Needs a pollinator variety nearby. Prune in late winter for best yield.
tasteDescription: Crisp and sweet with a pleasant tartness that varies by variety.
texture: Firm and crunchy with juicy flesh.
climateConditions: Needs cold winters for dormancy and cool, dry summers for best fruit quality.
growingTips: Requires cross-pollination from a compatible variety. Prune in late winter to encourage fruiting spurs.

name: Crab Apple
notes: Small tart fruits excellent for jelly and cider. Good pollinator for domestic apples.
tasteDescription: Intensely tart and astringent raw; transforms into bright, floral sweetness when cooked.
texture: Very firm and dense with minimal juice raw.
climateConditions: Hardy and adaptable; tolerates poor soils and exposed sites.
growingTips: Plant near domestic apple varieties to boost cross-pollination. Excellent wildlife tree.
healthBenefits: High in pectin for heart health

name: Pear
notes: Buttery, sweet flesh. Harvest before fully ripe and ripen indoors. Most varieties need a pollinator.
tasteDescription: Buttery and honey-sweet with floral notes; more complex than apple.
texture: Silky and melting with a slightly grainy core near the seeds.
climateConditions: Prefers deep, well-drained loam; sensitive to late frosts when in blossom.
growingTips: Harvest while still firm; ripen at room temperature. Needs cross-pollinator from same pollination group.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin C and K

name: Asian Pear
notes: Crisp, juicy texture unlike European pears. Ripens on tree. Self-fertile but yields improve with pollinator.
tasteDescription: Mild, lightly sweet with a clean, refreshing finish — less complex than European pear.
texture: Crunchy and exceptionally juicy; apple-like in firmness.
climateConditions: Tolerates more summer heat than European pear; needs adequate chill hours.
growingTips: Thin fruit aggressively — one fruit per spur — for best size and flavour.

name: Quince
notes: Hard and astringent raw; transforms into fragrant, honey-gold flesh when cooked. Excellent for jams and paste.
tasteDescription: Intensely floral and fruity when cooked; honey and rose notes with a lingering tartness.
texture: Rock-hard raw; becomes tender and jammy after long cooking.
climateConditions: Tolerates heavier, wetter soils than most fruit trees. Needs full sun.
growingTips: Self-fertile. Harvest after first frost for best flavour. Needs minimal pruning once established.

name: Sweet Cherry
notes: Rich, sweet flavour. Most varieties need a cross-pollinator. Birds are the main competition.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet with a deep, wine-like richness in dark varieties.
texture: Firm and juicy with a smooth, snapping skin.
climateConditions: Needs cold winters and dry summers; wet weather at harvest causes splitting.
growingTips: Net trees before ripening to beat birds. Grow on dwarfing rootstock for easier harvesting.

name: Sour Cherry
notes: Tart and bright; ideal for pies and jam. Self-fertile. More cold-hardy than sweet cherry.
tasteDescription: Sharply tart with a bright, fruity acidity; outstanding in cooked preparations.
texture: Soft and very juicy with thin skin.
climateConditions: Very cold-hardy; tolerates partial shade better than sweet cherries.
growingTips: Self-fertile — plant even one tree for a harvest. Prune to maintain an open centre for air circulation.

name: Plum
notes: Sweet to tart depending on variety. Many European plums are self-fertile; Japanese plums need pollinators.
tasteDescription: Sweet and tangy with rich plum and honey notes; great raw or cooked.
texture: Juicy and yielding with a thin, slightly waxy skin.
climateConditions: Tolerates a range of soils; needs full sun and adequate moisture.
growingTips: Thin fruit to avoid biennial bearing. Protect blossom from late frosts with fleece.

name: Japanese Plum
notes: Juicy, larger fruits than European plum. Needs cross-pollination. Blooms early — frost risk in cold climates.
tasteDescription: Sweeter and juicier than European plum with a tropical, floral undertone.
texture: Very juicy with firm flesh and a crisp bite when fresh.
climateConditions: Needs long warm growing seasons; blooms early so late frost is a risk.
growingTips: Plant with another Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination. Thin heavily for large fruit.

name: Damson
notes: Small, intensely flavoured blue-black plum. Self-fertile. Classic for jams, gin infusions and cheese.
tasteDescription: Intensely tart and astringent raw with a deep, winey flavour complexity when cooked.
texture: Small and firm with dense flesh clinging to the stone.
climateConditions: Extremely hardy and tolerant of exposed, northerly sites better than most stone fruit.
growingTips: Largely self-fertile. Prolific bearer — stake young trees to prevent branch breakage under heavy crops.

name: Greengage
notes: Sweet, honeyed flesh with complex floral notes. One of the finest dessert plums. Needs warm sheltered site.
tasteDescription: Exceptional honeyed sweetness with floral, almost perfumed depth — the finest dessert plum.
texture: Soft, juicy, and meltingly tender when fully ripe.
climateConditions: Needs a warm, sheltered wall in northern climates; ideal in Mediterranean-style summers.
growingTips: Fan-train against a south-facing wall for best results. Partially self-fertile but benefits from a pollinator.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamin A and C

name: Peach
notes: Soft, fragrant, sweet-juicy. Self-fertile. Susceptible to peach leaf curl; plant in sheltered spots.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet with a rich, musky fragrance and bright underlying acidity.
texture: Yielding and juicy with velvet skin and a clear separation from the stone when ripe.
climateConditions: Needs hot summers and mild winters; protect blossom from frost and leaves from rain to prevent curl.
growingTips: Fan-train against a warm wall. Spray copper fungicide before bud burst to prevent leaf curl.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin A and C

name: Nectarine
notes: Smooth-skinned peach with slightly more intense flavour. Self-fertile. Needs warm summers to ripen well.
tasteDescription: Slightly more intense and concentrated than peach; sweet with a clean, acidic finish.
texture: Firm and smooth-skinned; less downy and slightly crisper than peach.
climateConditions: Requires more warmth than peach to ripen well; prone to brown rot in wet summers.
growingTips: Thin fruits to 15 cm apart for best size. Grow under glass in cool, wet climates.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamins A, C, and E

name: Apricot
notes: Sweet, fragrant, low-acid fruit. Self-fertile but erratic yields. Blooms very early — frost is the main risk.
tasteDescription: Delicate, honey-sweet with a mild floral perfume and low acidity.
texture: Velvety skin with juicy, yielding flesh and a freestone.
climateConditions: Needs dry summers and cold winters; early blossom is extremely frost-sensitive.
growingTips: Fan-train against a sheltered south wall. Protect blossom with fleece in early spring.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamins A and C

name: Sloe (Blackthorn)
notes: Very tart small berry, best after first frost. Classic for sloe gin. Dense thorny shrub, good wildlife habitat.
tasteDescription: Harshly astringent and tart raw; deep, damson-like richness after frost and maceration.
texture: Firm and dry raw; softens significantly after frost.
climateConditions: Extremely tough; thrives on exposed chalk downlands and hedgerows.
growingTips: Harvest after first frost or freeze picked berries overnight to mimic frost's softening effect.

name: Medlar
notes: Must be 'bletted' (frosted and softened) before eating. Spiced-apple flavour. Self-fertile ornamental tree.
tasteDescription: Spiced apple with notes of cinnamon and brown sugar; unique and complex.
texture: Grainy and custard-soft when fully bletted; inedible when hard.
climateConditions: Tolerates heavy, wet soils and exposed sites; extremely cold-hardy once established.
growingTips: Harvest after first frost and store on straw, open end down, until flesh gives to pressure.

name: Loquat
notes: Mild, sweet-tart citrus-like flavour. Evergreen. Fruits in winter/spring when little else is available.
tasteDescription: Mild and sweet with a pleasant tartness; flavour hints of apricot, peach, and citrus.
texture: Smooth and juicy with a slight firmness; large seeds occupy much of the fruit.
climateConditions: Evergreen; tolerates light frost to -10°C when established. Prefers mild, humid winters.
growingTips: Thin clusters to 5–6 fruit for larger size. Self-fertile; a single tree bears well.

name: Fig
notes: Rich, honey-sweet. Self-fertile. Root restriction improves fruiting. Can be grown in containers in cooler zones.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet, honey-like, with jammy notes and a complex, earthy depth.
texture: Soft and yielding with a jammy interior filled with tiny seeds; skin is edible.
climateConditions: Thrives in hot, dry Mediterranean conditions; needs a warm wall in cooler climates.
growingTips: Restrict roots in a large pot or paved pit to encourage fruiting. Remove embryo figs in autumn.

name: Mulberry
notes: Deep burgundy berries with raspberry-blackberry flavour. Long-lived tree. Stains everything — harvest carefully.
tasteDescription: Deep, winey sweetness with blackberry and raspberry notes; uniquely complex.
texture: Soft and very juicy; bursts on contact — impossible to transport without bruising.
climateConditions: Tolerant of urban conditions and varied soils; needs full sun for best flavour.
growingTips: Spread a sheet below to harvest fruit as it drops. Long-lived tree improves with age.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamins C and K

name: Persimmon
notes: Non-astringent varieties (Fuyu) eaten crisp; astringent varieties (Hachiya) need to be fully soft. Very ornamental.
tasteDescription: Rich, pumpkin-like sweetness with caramel notes; incredibly sweet when fully ripe.
texture: Crisp like an apple (Fuyu) or custard-soft and jelly-like (Hachiya) when ripe.
climateConditions: Needs hot summers and mild winters; moderate drought tolerance once established.
growingTips: Do not harvest astringent varieties until fully soft. Fuyu can be eaten firm. Largely self-fertile.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin C and B6

name: American Persimmon
notes: Small but intensely sweet after frost. Very cold-hardy. Astringent until fully ripe. Good wildlife food source.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet, almost date-like, with brown sugar and spice notes after frost.
texture: Mealy and soft when ripe; astringent and dry until fully frosted.
climateConditions: Native to eastern North America; thrives in well-drained forest soils and tolerates dry spells.
growingTips: Needs male and female trees for fruit, or select a self-fertile cultivar. Harvest after hard frost.

name: Pawpaw
notes: Custardy, tropical-tasting — banana-mango-vanilla. Needs cross-pollination from another unrelated tree. Short shelf life.
tasteDescription: Creamy and tropical — banana, mango, and vanilla custard in one unforgettable mouthful.
texture: Soft and custard-like; scoopable directly from the skin like a pudding.
climateConditions: Native to temperate forest understory; tolerates shade when young but fruits best in full sun.
growingTips: Plant two genetically distinct trees. Fruit bruises easily and must be eaten within days of harvest.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamins C and A

name: Elderberry
notes: Tiny, tart berries — must be cooked before eating. Flowers also edible. Fast-growing native shrub/small tree.
tasteDescription: Deep, earthy-sweet with a musky, grapey undertone; flowers are delicate and muscat-scented.
texture: Tiny, juicy, and slightly gritty; seeds noticeable raw.
climateConditions: Highly adaptable; thrives in moist soils at woodland edges and hedgerows.
growingTips: Never eat raw — cook berries and discard raw seeds. Prune hard annually to maintain productive young growth.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamins C and A

name: Hawthorn
notes: Small mealy red haws. Edible but bland — best for hedgerow jelly. Excellent wildlife habitat and windbreak.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and slightly mealy raw; good flavour extracted into jelly with apple.
texture: Mealy and dry with large seed; not appealing to eat raw.
climateConditions: Extremely hardy; thrives in any exposure, poor soils, and coastal conditions.
growingTips: Best used for wildlife habitat and windbreak. Berries are valuable winter food for birds.

name: Rowan (Mountain Ash)
notes: Bitter orange-red berries — unpalatable raw but excellent jelly with game. Cold-hardy ornamental. Birds love them.
tasteDescription: Bitter and astringent raw; transforms into a sharp, vibrant jelly with beautiful colour.
texture: Small, firm, and slightly waxy; densely clustered.
climateConditions: One of the most cold-hardy fruiting trees; thrives at altitude and in harsh northern climates.
growingTips: Best harvested after first frost to reduce bitterness. Pair with crab apple in jelly recipes.
healthBenefits: Parasorbic acid converts to beneficial compounds when cooked

name: Sea Buckthorn
notes: Incredibly tart orange berries loaded with vitamin C. Nitrogen-fixer. Needs male and female plants.
tasteDescription: Explosively sour and astringent; fruity, citrus-like, and intensely flavoured.
texture: Soft and very juicy; bursts with tart juice when pressed.
climateConditions: Thrives in coastal, windswept sites and sandy soils; nitrogen-fixing roots improve poor soils.
growingTips: Plant one male to every six female plants. Harvest with gloved hands — thorns and juice stain.
healthBenefits: One of the highest Vitamin C contents of any fruit
Supports skin and mucous membrane health

name: Gooseberry
notes: Tart when unripe (for cooking); sweet and complex when fully ripe. Self-fertile. Tolerates partial shade.
tasteDescription: Sharp and tart when green; honey-sweet with floral and grape notes when fully golden-ripe.
texture: Firm and crisp with a thin, translucent skin that softens at full ripeness.
climateConditions: Cool and moist; one of the few fruits that tolerates partial shade and north-facing aspects.
growingTips: Pick green for cooking in May; leave to ripen fully yellow for dessert use in July–August.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin A and E

name: Red Currant
notes: Bright, tart, jewel-like clusters. Self-fertile. Great for jelly, summer pudding. Tolerates partial shade well.
tasteDescription: Sharply tart and fresh with a clean berry acidity that brightens any dish.
texture: Tiny, pop-in-the-mouth berries with glossy, translucent skin and many seeds.
climateConditions: Cool and moist; excellent north-facing wall plant. Dislikes hot, dry summers.
growingTips: Harvest entire strigs intact with a fork to avoid bruising. Freeze whole for year-round use.

name: Blackcurrant
notes: Intensely aromatic, tart berries — highest vitamin C of any currant. Self-fertile. Prune hard for best yield.
tasteDescription: Intensely aromatic and tart with a unique, deeply complex perfumed darkness.
texture: Firm skin bursting with intensely flavoured juice; aromatic even before tasting.
climateConditions: Prefers cooler, moister climates; tolerates frost well but blossom susceptible to late frosts.
growingTips: Cut one third of oldest stems to the ground each winter to stimulate vigorous new fruiting growth.
healthBenefits: Highest Vitamin C of all common fruits

name: White Currant
notes: Milder, sweeter than red currant. Self-fertile. Beautiful translucent fruits. Great for fresh eating.
tasteDescription: Delicate and mildly sweet; less acidic than red currant with a clean, refreshing finish.
texture: Translucent, jewel-like berries; slightly softer and juicier than red currant.
climateConditions: Same requirements as red currant; excellent in partial shade.
growingTips: Best eaten fresh; the flavour is too delicate to survive heavy cooking or preserving.

name: Jostaberry
notes: Blackcurrant-gooseberry hybrid. Large, sweet-tart dark berries. Disease-resistant, vigorous, self-fertile.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart cross between blackcurrant and gooseberry with good depth of flavour.
texture: Larger than currant; firm with blackcurrant-like juice.
climateConditions: Very adaptable and disease-resistant; good choice for organic gardens.
growingTips: Vigorous grower — give plenty of space. Largely immune to big bud mite and leaf spot.
healthBenefits: Combines benefits of both parent fruits

name: Blackberry
notes: Rich, earthy-sweet. Self-fertile. Thorned or thornless varieties. Aggressive spreader — manage suckers.
tasteDescription: Deep, earthy sweetness with a rich winey complexity; tart when under-ripe.
texture: Soft and juicy with many small drupelets; stains deeply.
climateConditions: Extremely adaptable; thrives in hedgerows, disturbed ground, and woodland edges.
growingTips: Tie new canes to wires as they grow; cut fruited canes to the ground after harvest.
healthBenefits: Very high in Vitamin C and K

name: Raspberry
notes: Delicate, perfumed, sweet-tart. Summer and autumn-fruiting varieties available. Self-fertile. Needs good drainage.
tasteDescription: Delicate, intensely perfumed sweetness with a bright, clean acidity.
texture: Extremely soft and fragile; hollow interior filled with tiny drupelets.
climateConditions: Prefers cool, moist summers; dislikes drought and waterlogged soils.
growingTips: Autumn-fruiting varieties are easiest — cut all canes to ground in February.

name: Strawberry
notes: Sweet, fragrant. Perpetual varieties fruit spring to autumn. Replace plants every 3–4 years for best yields.
tasteDescription: The quintessential summer sweetness; intensely aromatic with a balance of sugar and acidity.
texture: Juicy and yielding; skin is thin and fragile.
climateConditions: Adaptable to most climates; needs shelter from heavy rain to prevent grey mould at fruiting time.
growingTips: Tuck straw under developing fruit to keep clean. Replace runners every 3–4 years. Net to protect from birds.

name: Blueberry
notes: Sweet with slight tartness. Needs acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5). Plant two varieties for best cross-pollination.
tasteDescription: Mild and sweet with a hint of tartness; flavour intensifies dramatically when home-grown.
texture: Firm and round with a dusty blue bloom; bursts with juice.
climateConditions: Requires acidic, moisture-retentive soil; prefers cool, humid summers.
growingTips: Acidify soil with sulphur chips and ericaceous compost. Pair two different varieties for best yields.
healthBenefits: One of the highest antioxidant fruits

name: Cranberry
notes: Very tart. Requires consistently moist, acidic, peaty soil. Usually grown on low-lying bogs. Self-fertile.
tasteDescription: Intensely tart and astringent; almost inedible raw but brilliant in sauces and juices.
texture: Firm and round; bounces when ripe (the traditional float test).
climateConditions: Native to boggy, acidic northern habitats; requires consistently moist, peaty, acidic soil.
growingTips: Mulch heavily with acidic pine bark. Excellent in large containers with ericaceous compost.

name: Lingonberry
notes: Tart, astringent red berries — classic Scandinavian preserve. Evergreen groundcover. Very cold-hardy.
tasteDescription: Sharp, cranberry-like tartness with a fruity, slightly bitter depth.
texture: Small, firm, and waxy; very juicy when crushed.
climateConditions: Arctic-hardy native of boreal forests; needs acidic, well-drained soil and cool temperatures.
growingTips: Excellent groundcover under acid-loving shrubs. Virtually maintenance-free once established.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamins C and E

name: Bilberry
notes: Smaller and more intensely flavoured than blueberry. Dark flesh stains deeply. Grows on moorland and heathland.
tasteDescription: Far more intense and complex than blueberry; deep winey flavour with earthier, forest notes.
texture: Small and soft; stains everything deep purple — including teeth.
climateConditions: Native to acidic moorland and heath; very difficult to cultivate outside its natural habitat.
growingTips: Best harvested wild in late summer on upland heathland. Very difficult to grow in gardens.
healthBenefits: Supports eye health and night vision
High in Vitamin C and manganese

name: Honeyberry (Haskap)
notes: First soft fruit of the season. Elongated blue berry, blueberry-raspberry flavour. Needs two compatible varieties.
tasteDescription: Complex and variable — blueberry-raspberry with hints of black cherry; some varieties more tart.
texture: Elongated and firm; pulp similar to blueberry.
climateConditions: Extremely cold-hardy Arctic species; actually benefits from very cold winters for best yields.
growingTips: Plant two varieties with overlapping bloom times for cross-pollination. Among the very first fruits of the year.

name: Goji Berry
notes: Mildly sweet, slightly herbal. Extremely hardy and drought-tolerant once established. Self-fertile.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and slightly herbal; somewhere between cranberry and cherry with a subtle earthiness.
texture: Slightly chewy when fresh; dried berries are raisin-like.
climateConditions: Drought-tolerant once established; tolerates poor, alkaline soils and coastal conditions.
growingTips: Train as a standard or allow to scramble. Incredibly productive — one plant yields kilograms of berries.
healthBenefits: Rich in zeaxanthin for eye health

name: Autumn Olive
notes: Sweet-tart speckled red berries, high in lycopene. Nitrogen-fixer. Invasive in some US regions — check local rules.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart with a light astringency; speckled red berries taste of cranberry and cherry.
texture: Small and juicy with a soft flesh and one central seed.
climateConditions: Adaptable nitrogen-fixer; thrives in poor soils. Check invasive status in your region before planting.
growingTips: Do not plant where invasive (eastern US). Excellent pioneer plant and wildlife food source elsewhere.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin C and E

name: Cornelian Cherry
notes: Tart, olive-shaped red fruit — delicious jam and fruit leather. Ornamental spring-flowering tree. Very long-lived.
tasteDescription: Tart and tangy with a cherry-sour vibrancy; cooked fruit reveals a rich, jammy complexity.
texture: Firm and slightly astringent raw; olive-like with a long central stone.
climateConditions: Tough and adaptable; among the first trees to flower in late winter. Tolerates alkaline soils.
growingTips: Harvest when deep red and beginning to soften. Makes exceptional jam and fruit leather.

name: Walnut
notes: Rich, oily nut with slightly bitter skin. Large tree — allow 10 m+ space. Juglone inhibits some nearby plants.
tasteDescription: Rich, buttery, and slightly bitter with complex earthy depth; freshly cracked walnuts are transformatively good.
texture: Dense and oily; papery skin around kernel adds astringency.
climateConditions: Needs deep, well-drained soil and full sun; late frost damages new growth — choose a sheltered site.
growingTips: Allow 10 m between trees and structures. Keep away from vegetable beds due to juglone allelopathy.

name: Black Walnut
notes: Stronger, earthier flavour than English walnut. Strong juglone allelopathy — keep away from vegetable gardens.
tasteDescription: Bolder, more pungent and earthy than English walnut with a distinctive, smoky intensity.
texture: Dense and oily; very hard shell requiring a mallet.
climateConditions: Tough native tree; tolerates poor soils and drought once established.
growingTips: Extremely difficult to crack — use a vice or dedicated cracker. Strong juglone: avoid near gardens.

name: Hazelnut (Cobnut)
notes: Sweet, mild nut. Needs cross-pollination from another variety. Can be coppiced to maintain shrub form.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and milky when fresh; deepens into rich, toasted complexity when dried.
texture: Crunchy when dried; tender and almost milky when freshly harvested.
climateConditions: Hardy and adaptable to most soils; wind-pollinated so no need for insect pollinators.
growingTips: Plant two or more varieties for cross-pollination. Coppice on rotation to renew productive growth.

name: Sweet Chestnut
notes: Starchy, sweet nut — roasted or used in flour. Large tree. Needs another chestnut nearby for good nut set.
tasteDescription: Sweet, starchy, and earthy; roasting unlocks a caramel-like depth that is intensely seasonal.
texture: Dense and starchy like potato when raw; becomes soft and floury when cooked.
climateConditions: Prefers acidic, well-drained sandy or loamy soils; intolerant of chalk and waterlogging.
growingTips: Plant two or more trees for good cross-pollination. Harvest after spiny cases split and nuts fall.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin C (unique among nuts)

name: Almond
notes: Needs long hot summers to ripen. Most varieties need cross-pollination. Grown for nut and ornamental blossom.
tasteDescription: Sweet and milky with a distinctive marzipan-like richness; bitter varieties are inedible raw.
texture: Crunchy and dense; papery inner skin adds mild astringency.
climateConditions: Needs long, hot, dry summers and mild winters. Blossom is extremely frost-sensitive.
growingTips: Train against a warm south wall in cooler climates. Self-fertile varieties (e.g. Robijn) are available.

name: Olive
notes: Intensely bitter until cured; then fruity and rich. Needs hot dry summers and cold winters to flower.
tasteDescription: Intensely bitter raw; cured olives range from mild and buttery to complex and pungent.
texture: Firm and waxy with an oily flesh around a hard central stone.
climateConditions: Needs hot, dry Mediterranean summers and cold (but frost-free) winters to initiate flowering.
growingTips: Shelter from hard frost. Container-grown trees can be brought indoors in winter in colder zones.

name: Lemon
notes: Tart, aromatic. Can fruit continuously. Grown in containers in cool climates — bring indoors before frost.
tasteDescription: Sharply acidic and intensely aromatic; the fresh zest is as valuable as the juice.
texture: Juicy and pulpy with a thick, aromatic rind.
climateConditions: Frost-tender; needs warmth year-round. Ideal for container growing in conservatories.
growingTips: Feed with citrus fertiliser every two weeks in summer. Re-pot every two years to maintain vigour.

name: Orange (Sweet)
notes: Sweet, juicy. Needs heat to develop sugar. Self-fertile. Container-grown trees possible in warm conservatories.
tasteDescription: Classic sweet citrus with a bright, uplifting acidity and floral perfume.
texture: Juicy and segmented with an aromatic rind.
climateConditions: Needs sustained heat and full sun for sugar development; frost-tender.
growingTips: Grow in large containers (minimum 40 cm pot) and move indoors in autumn in northern climates.
healthBenefits: Rich in flavonoids for heart health

name: Blood Orange
notes: Dramatic crimson flesh, raspberry-citrus flavour. Anthocyanin pigment develops best with cool nights.
tasteDescription: Sweet orange base with a distinctive raspberry-berry overlay; deeply complex and flavourful.
texture: Standard orange texture; the dramatic pigmentation is in the juice and flesh.
climateConditions: Needs cool nights (below 10°C) to develop anthocyanin pigmentation; unique among citrus.
growingTips: The cooler the nights during ripening, the deeper the red colour. Excellent juice variety.
healthBenefits: Rich in anthocyanin antioxidants (unique to blood oranges)

name: Clementine
notes: Easy-peel, sweet and seedless. More cold-tolerant than oranges. Good for container culture.
tasteDescription: Sweet, clean, and refreshing with a mild citrus perfume and no bitterness.
texture: Easy-peel loose skin with seedless, juicy segments.
climateConditions: More cold-tolerant than most citrus; one of the best for container growing in temperate climates.
growingTips: One of the easiest citrus for container culture. Self-fertile and extremely productive.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamin C and folate

name: Grapefruit
notes: Tart to sweet, slight bitterness. Large tree. Needs 18 months from flower to ripe fruit.
tasteDescription: Refreshingly tart with a characteristic pleasant bitterness; pink varieties are sweeter.
texture: Very juicy with thick pith; segments are large and succulent.
climateConditions: Needs the most heat of all common citrus to develop sweetness; thrives in Florida and California.
growingTips: Pink and ruby varieties are sweeter and more popular. Slow to ripen — needs 12–18 months.
healthBenefits: Interacts with some medications — check before use

name: Meyer Lemon
notes: Sweeter and less acidic than true lemon. Thin-skinned. Popular container citrus. More cold-tolerant.
tasteDescription: Gentler than true lemon; sweet-tart balance with floral, almost mandarin-like notes.
texture: Thin-skinned with abundant, sweet juice and fewer seeds.
climateConditions: More cold-tolerant than true lemon; ideal for container growing in temperate climates.
growingTips: Among the best citrus for pot culture; fragrant flowers make it an excellent houseplant.

name: Lime
notes: Very tart and intensely aromatic. Least cold-tolerant citrus. Excellent in containers with winter protection.
tasteDescription: Sharper and more intensely aromatic than lemon; distinctive tropical citrus perfume.
texture: Very juicy with thin skin and abundant seeds.
climateConditions: Most frost-tender citrus; needs tropical or subtropical warmth year-round.
growingTips: Bring containers indoors at first frost. Protect from any cold draughts.

name: Kumquat
notes: Eaten whole — sweet peel, tart flesh. Most cold-hardy citrus relative. Ornamental and prolific.
tasteDescription: Unique inside-out citrus experience: sweet, floral rind contrasts with tart, sour interior.
texture: Firm rind eaten intact; the contrast of textures is part of the appeal.
climateConditions: Most cold-hardy citrus relative; tolerates light frost to around -8°C when established.
growingTips: Eat the whole fruit — the sweet peel is the point. Excellent ornamental container plant.
healthBenefits: Rich in plant flavonoids in the peel

name: Pomegranate
notes: Tart-sweet jewel-like arils. Needs hot summers. Drought-tolerant once established. Long-lived ornamental.
tasteDescription: Complex and sweet-tart with a refreshing astringency; arils burst with deep fruity juice.
texture: Crunchy, juicy arils each encasing a seed; the seeds are edible.
climateConditions: Thrives in hot, dry Mediterranean conditions; surprisingly cold-tolerant to -12°C once established.
growingTips: Harvest when skin begins to split. Drought-tolerant once established. Beautiful ornamental year-round.

name: Avocado
notes: Creamy, rich. Needs two trees (type A and type B) for reliable fruiting. Very frost-sensitive.
tasteDescription: Buttery and rich with a delicate, nutty creaminess and neutral flavour.
texture: Smooth and creamy — almost spreadable; texture depends greatly on ripeness.
climateConditions: Frost-tender; needs warmth and humidity. California and Florida varieties have different requirements.
growingTips: Plant a type A and type B for best yields. Avocados ripen off the tree — harvest when full-sized.
healthBenefits: Contains Vitamins K, C, B5 and B6

name: Guava
notes: Fragrant, sweet-tart tropical fruit. Self-fertile. Fast-growing. Can be kept as a container shrub in cooler zones.
tasteDescription: Intensely fragrant and tropical; sweet-tart flavour that combines strawberry, pear, and citrus.
texture: Granular and seedy interior with smooth, thin skin; very aromatic.
climateConditions: Frost-tender but adaptable; thrives in tropical and subtropical conditions.
growingTips: Self-fertile and incredibly productive. Can be container-grown and brought indoors in winter.
healthBenefits: One of the highest Vitamin C fruits — 4× more than orange

name: Feijoa (Pineapple Guava)
notes: Unique pineapple-mint-guava flavour. Edible flowers. Reasonably cold-hardy. Needs cross-pollinator for best yields.
tasteDescription: Unique tropical complexity: pineapple, mint, guava, and eucalyptus all at once.
texture: Gritty and granular interior with smooth, thin green skin; flesh scooped out with a spoon.
climateConditions: Reasonably cold-hardy to -12°C; thrives in mild, maritime climates.
growingTips: Plant two different varieties for cross-pollination. Edible flowers are sweet and delicious.
healthBenefits: High in iodine — rare for fruit

name: Banana
notes: Sweet, starchy. Each stem flowers once; cut after harvest and let suckers take over. Needs warmth and moisture.
tasteDescription: Sweet, starchy, and mellow; flavour intensifies dramatically as the skin yellows and spots.
texture: Soft and starchy; creamy-textured with no seeds in cultivated varieties.
climateConditions: Needs warmth, humidity, and wind protection; the pseudostem dies after fruiting.
growingTips: Cut fruited stems to the ground to allow suckers to take over. Mulch heavily in cooler zones.
healthBenefits: Rich in potassium for heart health
Contains Vitamin B6 for brain function

name: Grape (Table)
notes: Sweet, thin-skinned. Train on a sunny wall or pergola. Prune hard in winter. Many varieties available.
tasteDescription: Sweet and fruity with a range of flavour profiles from neutral to muscat-aromatic.
texture: Juicy and thin-skinned; seedless varieties offer the best eating experience.
climateConditions: Needs full sun and warmth for sugar development; tolerates most well-drained soils.
growingTips: Spur-prune hard each winter to two buds per rod. Thin bunches to improve size and air circulation.

name: Kiwi (Hardy)
notes: Small, smooth-skinned, grape-sized. Eaten whole. Very vigorous climber. Needs male and female plants.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet and aromatic; far better flavour concentration than standard kiwi.
texture: Smooth-skinned and grape-sized; eaten whole without peeling.
climateConditions: Very cold-hardy; needs a strong, sturdy support structure for its vigorous growth.
growingTips: One male plant pollinates up to eight females. Train on a pergola — can grow 10 m in a season.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin K and folate
Contains actinidin enzyme for protein digestion

name: Passion Fruit
notes: Intensely fragrant, tart-sweet pulp. Fast-growing vine. Fruits wrinkle when ripe — don't harvest too early.
tasteDescription: Intensely aromatic and tart-sweet; among the most perfumed of all fruits.
texture: Gelatinous pulp surrounding edible seeds; the contrast of slippery and crunchy is appealing.
climateConditions: Frost-tender; needs warmth and shelter. Grows fast and produces prolifically in warm climates.
growingTips: Harvest only when the skin begins to wrinkle — this signals peak ripeness and sweetness.
healthBenefits: Very high in Vitamins A and C

name: Serviceberry (Juneberry)
notes: Sweet, almond-scented berries. Among the first soft fruits of the season. Native wildlife magnet. Self-fertile.
tasteDescription: Sweet with a distinctive almond note; one of the most pleasant flavours among native fruits.
texture: Soft and juicy; similar to blueberry but with a softer skin.
climateConditions: Native to woodland edges and stream banks; tolerates partial shade and various soil types.
growingTips: Among the first fruits of the season. Beautiful spring blossom and autumn colour make it highly ornamental.

name: Aronia (Chokeberry)
notes: Very tart and astringent raw; excellent dried or in juice. High in antioxidants. Self-fertile and very hardy.
tasteDescription: Very tart and astringent raw; deep, complex berry flavour when processed into juice or dried.
texture: Firm and dense; stains deeply like elderberry.
climateConditions: Exceptionally cold-hardy native shrub; tolerates wet soils and partial shade.
growingTips: Best processed — juice, dried, or jam. Exceptionally productive and virtually pest-free.
healthBenefits: Among the highest antioxidant-density fruits known

name: Hackberry
notes: Small sweet-date flavoured purple berries. Tough native tree, tolerates drought and poor soil. Wildlife tree.
tasteDescription: Sweet and date-like with a pleasant, mild complexity; underappreciated and largely foraged.
texture: Small with a large central seed; thin sweet flesh surrounds a hard stone.
climateConditions: Extremely tough; survives drought, compacted urban soils, salt spray, and extreme cold.
growingTips: Excellent urban and wildlife tree. Largely self-sufficient once established.
healthBenefits: Contains healthy fats in the seed
High in protein relative to other fruits

name: Alphonso (Hapus) Mango
notes: The king of mangoes; rich, saffron-colored, fibreless pulp.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet with a complex, fruity floral finish and hints of saffron.
texture: Smooth, creamy, and completely fibreless — melts in the mouth.
climateConditions: Thrives in tropical climates with a distinct dry season.
growingTips: Requires full sun and well-drained soil; avoid heavy humidity during flowering.

name: Kesar Mango
notes: Known for vibrant saffron color and intense aroma.
tasteDescription: Sweet and honey-rich with an intense saffron-mango aroma; less fibre than Alphonso.
texture: Smooth and creamy; slightly more fibrous than Alphonso.
climateConditions: Thrives in semi-arid tropical conditions of Gujarat; needs distinct wet and dry seasons.
growingTips: Best in dry, warm climates. Avoid overwatering; good drainage is essential.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin A and C

name: Kent Mango
notes: Large, sweet, and juicy; excellent backyard variety for Florida.
tasteDescription: Mild and sweet with low acidity; clean mango flavour with minimal fibre.
texture: Smooth and very juicy with minimal fibre.
climateConditions: Tolerates South Florida subtropical humidity; needs good air circulation to prevent fungal issues.
growingTips: Excellent Florida backyard tree; prune after harvest to maintain manageable size.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamin C and A

name: Keitt Mango
notes: Late-season producer; keeps green even when ripe.
tasteDescription: Sweet and fruity; milder than Alphonso but refreshing and good for late-season eating.
texture: Firm and moderately fibrous; holds up well for slicing.
climateConditions: Adaptable to South Florida conditions; one of the last mangoes to ripen.
growingTips: Do not judge ripeness by colour — Keitt stays green. Use the squeeze test for ripeness.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamins A and C

name: Allahabad Safeda Guava
notes: Large, white-fleshed, extremely sweet and popular in India.
tasteDescription: Exceptionally sweet with delicate, almost vanilla-like sweetness; far milder than pink guava.
texture: Soft, white flesh with minimal grittiness; fewer seeds than other varieties.
climateConditions: Thrives in tropical and subtropical plains; tolerates drought once established.
growingTips: Best eaten fresh when just softening. Prolific bearer — thin fruit for larger size.

name: Beaumont Guava
notes: Heavy producer in Florida; pink flesh, great for juice.
tasteDescription: Tangy and aromatic pink flesh with strong guava fragrance; excellent for juice.
texture: Granular pink flesh with many seeds; best processed for juice or jam.
climateConditions: Adaptable to South Florida conditions; tolerates brief cold snaps.
growingTips: Prolific bearer. Best used for juice or jam; abundant seeds make fresh eating less appealing.
healthBenefits: One of the highest Vitamin C fruits

name: Chikoo (Sapodilla)
notes: Sweet, malt-like flavor; thrives in sandy Florida soil.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet with a unique malt, brown sugar, and pear drop flavour unlike any other fruit.
texture: Grainy and starchy texture when under-ripe; becomes smooth and custard-like when fully ripe.
climateConditions: Thrives in sandy, well-drained tropical soils; very drought-tolerant once established.
growingTips: Only harvest when a small area of brown skin scratches to reveal tan (not green) underneath.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamins A and C

name: Brewster Lychee
notes: Favorite Florida variety; produces large, juicy, sweet fruit.
tasteDescription: Floral, perfumed sweetness with a light acidity; rose-water and grape notes.
texture: Juicy and translucent white flesh around a central seed; enclosed in bumpy red skin.
climateConditions: Needs cool, dry winters to initiate flowering; does not tolerate frost or prolonged cold.
growingTips: Harvest in clusters. Needs a distinct cool-dry winter period to trigger blossom set.

name: Choquette Avocado
notes: Florida favorite; smooth, glossy skin, large size, creamy.
tasteDescription: Buttery and richly creamy with a clean, mild avocado flavour; less fatty than Hass.
texture: Smooth and creamy with a glossy, thin green skin; large with a small seed.
climateConditions: Adapted to Florida humidity and warmth; type B pollinator pairs well with type A varieties.
growingTips: Type B variety — pair with a type A (e.g. Lula) for best yields. Large tree needing space.
healthBenefits: Contains Vitamins K, C and B6
Supports nutrient absorption from other foods

name: Starfruit (Carambola)
notes: Prolific producer; crisp and tangy-sweet.
tasteDescription: Tangy-sweet with a refreshing juiciness; flavour combines apple, pear, and citrus.
texture: Crisp and juicy with a distinctive star cross-section; waxy, edible skin.
climateConditions: Thrives in tropical and subtropical conditions; tolerates brief dry periods.
growingTips: Self-fertile and prolific. Fruits twice yearly. Sweet varieties are better for fresh eating.
healthBenefits: Contains potassium and fibre. Note: toxic in high amounts to those with kidney disease

name: Jackfruit
notes: The world's largest tree fruit; versatile culinary staple.
tasteDescription: Ripe flesh is sweet and fruity with mango and banana notes; unripe flesh is starchy and neutral.
texture: Ripe: stringy and sweet; unripe: firm and meaty — a popular meat substitute.
climateConditions: Strictly tropical; needs heat, humidity, and well-drained deep soil.
growingTips: Extremely large fruit (up to 35 kg) needs support when young. Wear gloves when cutting.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamins B6 and C
Good plant-based protein source when unripe

name: Red Lady Papaya
notes: Fast-growing; bears fruit in less than a year.
tasteDescription: Sweet and musky with a tropical perfume; flesh is mild and refreshing.
texture: Smooth and buttery-soft; easily scooped from the skin with a spoon.
climateConditions: Needs warmth year-round; killed by frost. Thrives in tropical and subtropical conditions.
growingTips: Fruits within 9–11 months of seed. Replace every 2–3 years as productivity declines with age.
healthBenefits: Contains papain enzyme for protein digestion

name: Dasheri Mango
notes: Classic North Indian mango from the Malihabad belt near Lucknow. Elongated, fibreless, intensely fragrant.
tasteDescription: Very sweet with a rich, perfumed aroma and almost no tartness.
texture: Smooth, fibreless, melting flesh.
climateConditions: Thrives in hot, dry subtropical summers with a distinct dry season before fruiting.
growingTips: Grafted trees fruit in 3–5 years. Withhold irrigation before flowering to boost bloom.

name: Langra Mango
notes: Famous Varanasi mango that stays greenish even when ripe. Prized for its turpentine-tinged richness.
tasteDescription: Sweet and aromatic with a distinctive resinous, lemony note.
texture: Soft, fibreless and juicy.
climateConditions: Hot humid subtropical plains; needs monsoon moisture during fruit fill.
growingTips: Harvest when shoulders fill out though skin remains green. Prone to alternate bearing.

name: Chausa Mango
notes: Late-season golden-yellow mango from North India and Pakistan. Exceptionally sweet, often eaten by sucking the pulp.
tasteDescription: Honey-sweet and mild with low acidity and a luscious aroma.
texture: Very juicy, soft, nearly fibreless pulp.
climateConditions: Hot subtropical climate; tolerates the late summer heat that ripens it.
growingTips: One of the latest croppers, extending the mango season. Bag fruit to protect from fruit fly.
healthBenefits: Rich in Vitamin A and C

name: Banganapalli (Safeda) Mango
notes: Large oblong Andhra Pradesh mango, also called Safeda. A GI-tagged commercial variety with thin yellow skin.
tasteDescription: Sweet and mildly tangy with a clean, non-fibrous finish.
texture: Firm yet juicy, fibreless flesh.
climateConditions: Hot semi-arid South Indian climate with dry pre-harvest months.
growingTips: Heavy, reliable bearer. Thin fruit clusters for size and harvest at colour break.

name: Totapuri Mango
notes: Distinctive parrot-beak shaped South Indian mango used widely for pulp, juice and pickles.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and tangy with low sugar — more tart than dessert mangoes.
texture: Firm, fibreless and slightly crisp.
climateConditions: Hot tropical and semi-arid zones of southern India.
growingTips: Vigorous and productive; ideal for processing. Tolerates a range of soils.

name: Neelam Mango
notes: Small fragrant late-season mango widely grown across South India. Often the last mango of the season.
tasteDescription: Sweet and highly aromatic with a hint of citrus.
texture: Smooth, firm, fibreless flesh.
climateConditions: Adaptable across tropical South India; tolerates humid coastal heat.
growingTips: Compact tree suited to smaller gardens. Reliable annual bearer compared to many varieties.

name: Mallika Mango
notes: Hybrid of Neelam and Dasheri bred in India. A connoisseur's mango with deep orange flesh.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet with rich honey, citrus and melon notes.
texture: Dense, fibreless, buttery flesh.
climateConditions: Tropical to subtropical; performs well in both India and Florida.
growingTips: Semi-dwarf and well suited to container or backyard growing. Harvest firm and ripen off-tree.

name: Amrapali Mango
notes: Dwarf high-density hybrid (Dasheri x Neelam) developed by IARI. Popular for small orchards.
tasteDescription: Very sweet and rich with deep red-orange pulp.
texture: Fibreless, soft and juicy.
climateConditions: Tropical and subtropical India; suited to high-density planting.
growingTips: Naturally dwarf — plant closely. Regular bearer with high yield per acre.

name: Raspuri Mango
notes: Oval Karnataka mango known as the 'Queen of Mangoes', excellent for juices and smoothies.
tasteDescription: Sweet and juicy with a soft melting richness.
texture: Very juicy, smooth, slight fibre.
climateConditions: Tropical southern Deccan plateau climate.
growingTips: Best eaten fresh or pulped quickly as it does not store long. Harvest at full maturity.

name: Himsagar Mango
notes: Premium West Bengal mango with very high pulp-to-fruit ratio and no fibre.
tasteDescription: Richly sweet and creamy with a strong aroma.
texture: Completely fibreless, dense and smooth.
climateConditions: Humid subtropical eastern India (Bengal, Odisha).
growingTips: Short shelf life — consume soon after ripening. Susceptible to anthracnose in humidity.
healthBenefits: High in Vitamin A and C

name: Fazli Mango
notes: Large late-season Bengal/Bihar mango, often weighing over a kilo. Popular for pickles and amchur when raw.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet with a tangy edge; pleasant but not as rich as dessert types.
texture: Firm, somewhat fibrous, very fleshy.
climateConditions: Humid subtropical eastern plains.
growingTips: Vigorous large tree; excellent shade and heavy yields. Great dual-purpose variety.

name: Haden Mango
notes: Classic Florida mango from 1910 that parented many modern varieties. Brilliant red blush.
tasteDescription: Sweet with a rich, aromatic, slightly tart flavour.
texture: Firm with a little fibre near the seed.
climateConditions: Warm frost-free tropical/subtropical climate.
growingTips: Vigorous grower. Prone to alternate bearing and anthracnose in humid summers.

name: Tommy Atkins Mango
notes: The most common commercial export mango thanks to its durability and long shelf life.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet, lightly tangy — less aromatic than heirloom types.
texture: Firm and fibrous.
climateConditions: Tropical and subtropical; very tolerant of handling and storage.
growingTips: Heavy reliable bearer with good disease resistance. Excellent first tree for beginners.

name: Valencia Pride Mango
notes: A Haden seedling producing long, elegant fibreless fruit. A Florida favourite for backyard growers.
tasteDescription: Sweet and rich with a classic aromatic mango flavour.
texture: Smooth, fibreless, melting.
climateConditions: Warm frost-free climate; vigorous in Florida heat.
growingTips: Large vigorous tree — give it space or prune to size. Mid-to-late season cropper.

name: Nam Doc Mai Mango
notes: Premium Thai mango, superb eaten green with chilli-salt or fully ripe. Popular dooryard tree in Florida.
tasteDescription: Sweet and fragrant with a citrus-floral aroma when ripe.
texture: Fibreless, smooth and juicy.
climateConditions: Tropical lowland climate; highly heat tolerant.
growingTips: Suited to containers and small yards. Can produce two crops in ideal climates.

name: Carrie Mango
notes: Beloved Florida dwarf mango famous for intense flavour and disease resistance. Stays green when ripe.
tasteDescription: Exceptionally sweet and rich with a spicy, aromatic depth.
texture: Fibreless, soft and creamy.
climateConditions: Warm humid subtropical; notably anthracnose resistant.
growingTips: Naturally dwarf — ideal for containers and small gardens. Judge ripeness by softness and aroma, not colour.

name: Glenn Mango
notes: Early-season Florida mango with mild, crowd-pleasing flavour and good disease resistance.
tasteDescription: Sweet, mild and peachy with low fibre.
texture: Soft, fibreless and juicy.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical; reliable in Florida's humidity.
growingTips: Compact, manageable tree good for home growers. Consistent annual producer.

name: Ataulfo (Honey/Champagne) Mango
notes: Small golden kidney-shaped Mexican mango sold as Honey or Champagne mango. Buttery and fibreless.
tasteDescription: Very sweet with creamy honey and citrus notes.
texture: Smooth, buttery, completely fibreless.
climateConditions: Tropical climate; thrives in warm coastal heat.
growingTips: Thin-seeded with high edible yield. Skin wrinkles slightly when perfectly ripe.

name: Pink Guava
notes: Classic pink-fleshed guava grown across India and the tropics. Eaten fresh or as juice and jam.
tasteDescription: Sweet and musky-fragrant with a mild tang near the skin.
texture: Soft, granular flesh with edible seeds.
climateConditions: Tropical and subtropical; tolerates heat, humidity and brief dry spells.
growingTips: Fast-growing and precocious. Prune after harvest to control size and boost the next crop.

name: Thai White Guava
notes: Large crisp white-fleshed guava eaten firm and crunchy, often with chilli-salt.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and refreshing with a clean finish.
texture: Very crisp and crunchy, like a firm pear.
climateConditions: Warm tropical lowlands; heavy and continuous bearer.
growingTips: Bag fruit to deter fruit fly. Harvest while still firm for the signature crunch.

name: Custard Apple (Sitaphal)
notes: Known as Sitaphal in India. Heart-shaped fruit with sweet creamy segments around black seeds.
tasteDescription: Sweet and custardy with hints of vanilla and caramel.
texture: Soft, creamy, custard-like pulp.
climateConditions: Tropical and semi-arid; drought tolerant once established.
growingTips: Harvest when the skin segments separate slightly and yield to gentle pressure. Ripens off-tree.

name: Sugar Apple (Sharifa)
notes: Also called Sweetsop or Sharifa. Knobby green fruit that breaks into sweet creamy segments.
tasteDescription: Very sweet with a custardy, fragrant flavour.
texture: Soft, grainy-creamy pulp around glossy seeds.
climateConditions: Hot tropical and semi-arid; very heat and drought tolerant.
growingTips: Small tree ideal for backyards. Picks when segments loosen; ripens quickly off the tree.

name: Soursop (Lakshman Phal)
notes: Large spiny green fruit with fragrant fibrous pulp, popular for juices and ice creams.
tasteDescription: Tangy-sweet with notes of pineapple, strawberry and citrus.
texture: Soft, fibrous, cottony pulp.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropical; very frost sensitive.
growingTips: Protect from any cold. Harvest firm and let soften indoors. Strain pulp for juice.

name: Jamun (Black Plum)
notes: Indian black plum with deep purple astringent-sweet fruit famed for managing blood sugar.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart and astringent, staining the tongue purple.
texture: Juicy with a thin skin and single large seed.
climateConditions: Tropical and subtropical; tolerant of monsoon and heat.
growingTips: Large hardy shade tree. Harvest fully coloured fruit; eat fresh or make juice and vinegar.

name: Ber (Indian Jujube)
notes: Indian jujube producing crisp apple-like fruit on a hardy thorny tree. Extremely drought tolerant.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and tangy, apple-like when fresh.
texture: Crisp and crunchy ripening to mealy.
climateConditions: Hot arid and semi-arid; one of the most drought-hardy fruit trees.
growingTips: Thrives on neglect in poor soils. Prune thorny growth and harvest as fruit turns yellow-brown.

name: Bael (Wood Apple)
notes: Sacred Indian tree with a hard-shelled aromatic fruit traditionally made into sherbet.
tasteDescription: Sweet and aromatic with resinous, marmalade-like notes.
texture: Dense, sticky, pulpy interior with seeds.
climateConditions: Tropical and subtropical; tolerates drought and poor soils.
growingTips: Slow-growing hardy tree. Crack the woody shell and scoop pulp for drinks; remove seeds.

name: Wood Apple (Kawath)
notes: Hard greyish-shelled fruit with tangy brown pulp, used for chutneys and drinks in India.
tasteDescription: Tart and tangy with a fermented, tamarind-like sweetness.
texture: Sticky, granular brown pulp.
climateConditions: Hot tropical and semi-arid plains.
growingTips: Hardy and low-maintenance. Fruit is ripe when it falls; shake and scoop the aromatic pulp.

name: Tamarind (Imli)
notes: Large tropical tree producing brown pods of tangy pulp essential to Indian and global cooking.
tasteDescription: Intensely sour-sweet and tangy.
texture: Sticky fibrous pulp around hard seeds.
climateConditions: Hot tropical and semi-arid; very drought tolerant once mature.
growingTips: Long-lived majestic shade tree. Harvest pods when brittle; store pulp compressed.

name: Amla (Indian Gooseberry)
notes: Revered Ayurvedic fruit; small translucent-green berries extraordinarily rich in Vitamin C.
tasteDescription: Intensely sour and astringent with a sweet aftertaste.
texture: Hard, crisp and fibrous.
climateConditions: Tropical and subtropical; tolerates heat and moderate drought.
growingTips: Hardy tree once established. Usually pickled, candied or juiced rather than eaten raw.

name: Karonda (Bengal Currant)
notes: Thorny Indian shrub bearing clusters of tart berries used in pickles and preserves.
tasteDescription: Sharply sour when green, sweet-tart when fully ripe and dark.
texture: Crisp and juicy with small seeds.
climateConditions: Tropical and semi-arid; very hardy and drought tolerant.
growingTips: Makes an excellent thorny hedge. Harvest green for pickles, dark purple for fresh eating.

name: Phalsa
notes: Small purple summer berries from the Indian subcontinent, famous for cooling sherbet.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart and refreshing with a tangy bite.
texture: Juicy with a thin skin and small seed.
climateConditions: Hot semi-arid and tropical; thrives in intense summer heat.
growingTips: Prune hard in winter to encourage fruiting shoots. Harvest in multiple pickings as berries ripen.

name: Kokum
notes: Western Ghats fruit dried into dark rinds used as a souring agent in Konkani and coastal cuisine.
tasteDescription: Tart and tangy with a subtle sweetness.
texture: Fleshy rind, dried to leathery.
climateConditions: Humid tropical coastal climate of western India.
growingTips: Slow-growing evergreen. Sun-dry the rinds; the pulp also yields cooling kokum sherbet.

name: Mahua
notes: Central Indian tree whose sweet flowers are eaten, fermented and used in traditional foods.
tasteDescription: Flowers are sweet and honey-like; fruit mildly sweet.
texture: Fleshy fragrant flowers; oily seeds.
climateConditions: Tropical dry deciduous forests; very drought hardy.
growingTips: Large culturally important tree. Collect flowers as they drop at dawn; seeds yield oil.

name: Mauritius Lychee
notes: Popular lychee cultivar with red rough skin and fragrant translucent flesh.
tasteDescription: Sweet and floral with a mild rose-like aroma.
texture: Juicy, firm, translucent flesh.
climateConditions: Subtropical with cool dry winters and warm humid summers.
growingTips: Needs a brief cool period to flower. Protect from wind; harvest whole panicles when red.

name: Longan
notes: Relative of lychee with brown skin and sweet translucent flesh; called 'dragon eye'.
tasteDescription: Sweet and musky with a refreshing finish.
texture: Juicy, firm, translucent flesh around a dark seed.
climateConditions: Tropical and warm subtropical; more cold tolerant than lychee.
growingTips: Bears in large clusters. Harvest whole bunches when skin turns tan and flesh is sweet.

name: Rambutan
notes: Hairy red tropical fruit related to lychee with sweet juicy flesh.
tasteDescription: Sweet and mildly tart with a grape-like juiciness.
texture: Firm, juicy, translucent flesh.
climateConditions: Hot humid equatorial tropics; very frost sensitive.
growingTips: Needs consistent warmth and humidity. Harvest when skin is fully red and spines soften.

name: Mangosteen
notes: The 'queen of fruits' with thick purple rind and sweet snow-white segments.
tasteDescription: Sweet and tangy with delicate peach-citrus notes.
texture: Soft, juicy, melting white segments.
climateConditions: Hot humid equatorial tropics; extremely cold sensitive.
growingTips: Very slow-growing and demanding of humidity. Shade young trees; harvest when rind is deep purple.

name: Durian
notes: The pungent 'king of fruits' with spiky husk and rich custardy flesh.
tasteDescription: Intensely rich and sweet with savoury, oniony, almond undertones.
texture: Thick, creamy, custard-like flesh.
climateConditions: Hot humid equatorial tropics with high rainfall.
growingTips: Very large tree needing space and heat. Fruit drops when ripe; handle the spiny husk carefully.

name: Mamey Sapote
notes: Large brown-skinned fruit with salmon-coloured flesh popular in Latin shakes and ice cream.
tasteDescription: Sweet with flavours of sweet potato, pumpkin and almond.
texture: Smooth, creamy, dense flesh.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics; frost sensitive.
growingTips: Large tree; grafted plants fruit sooner. Test ripeness by scratching skin to reveal salmon flesh.

name: Black Sapote (Chocolate Pudding Fruit)
notes: Persimmon relative whose ripe brown flesh resembles chocolate pudding.
tasteDescription: Mild and sweet with a custardy, chocolate-pudding-like character.
texture: Soft, smooth, custardy when fully ripe.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics and subtropics; some cold tolerance once established.
growingTips: Harvest green and let soften until the skin browns and flesh turns dark. Eat with a spoon.

name: Canistel (Egg Fruit)
notes: Bright orange-yellow fruit with dry, mealy flesh resembling cooked egg yolk.
tasteDescription: Sweet and rich, like custard or sweet potato.
texture: Dry, smooth, mealy and dense.
climateConditions: Warm tropical and subtropical; moderately cold tolerant.
growingTips: Compact tree good for small yards. Ripen off-tree until soft; great in shakes and custards.

name: Star Fruit (Kamrakh)
notes: Ribbed fruit that cuts into star shapes; called Kamrakh in India. Eaten fresh or in chutney.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart and juicy with a grape-citrus character.
texture: Crisp, watery and crunchy.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics and subtropics.
growingTips: Productive small tree often fruiting multiple times a year. Harvest when ribs turn golden.

name: Bilimbi (Cucumber Tree)
notes: Relative of star fruit bearing small sour green fruits used in pickles, curries and chutneys.
tasteDescription: Very sour and tangy.
texture: Crisp and juicy.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics; needs consistent moisture.
growingTips: Fruits directly on trunk and branches in heavy clusters. Use fresh in cooking or preserve.

name: Jabuticaba
notes: Brazilian tree that fruits directly on its trunk with grape-like purple-black berries.
tasteDescription: Sweet and slightly tart, like a rich grape.
texture: Juicy gel-like pulp with thick skin.
climateConditions: Subtropical to warm temperate; tolerates light frost when mature.
growingTips: Slow-growing but long-lived. Fruits multiple times a year; eat fresh or make wine and jelly.

name: Miracle Fruit
notes: Small red berry that temporarily makes sour foods taste sweet.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet itself; alters taste perception so sour becomes sweet.
texture: Thin pulp around a single seed.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics; needs acidic soil.
growingTips: Grows well in containers with acidic mix. Eat the berry then taste a lemon for the effect.

name: Barbados Cherry (Acerola)
notes: Small bright-red cherry-like fruit among the richest natural sources of Vitamin C.
tasteDescription: Tart and tangy with mild sweetness.
texture: Soft and juicy.
climateConditions: Warm tropical and subtropical; tolerates some drought.
growingTips: Shrubby tree fruiting several times a year. Pick fully red and use quickly as it is perishable.

name: Surinam Cherry (Pitanga)
notes: Ribbed red-to-black fruit on a hardy ornamental hedge plant.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart and resinous; sweeter as it darkens.
texture: Soft and juicy.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical and tropical; quite hardy and adaptable.
growingTips: Excellent fruiting hedge. Let fruit ripen to deep red or black for best sweetness.

name: June Plum (Amra)
notes: Crunchy tropical fruit eaten green with salt-chilli or ripe; called Amra/Ambarella.
tasteDescription: Tangy and sweet with pineapple-mango notes.
texture: Crisp when green, softer and juicy when ripe.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics; frost sensitive.
growingTips: Fast-growing and productive. Harvest green for crunch or yellow for sweetness; fibrous seed.

name: Apple Ber (Thai Apple Jujube)
notes: Improved large-fruited jujube the size of a small apple, crisp and sweet.
tasteDescription: Sweet and crisp, like a cross between apple and pear.
texture: Very crunchy and juicy.
climateConditions: Hot semi-arid and tropical; highly drought tolerant.
growingTips: Grafts fruit very young. Bag fruit against fruit fly; harvest at pale green to yellow.

name: Pomelo (Chakotra)
notes: Largest citrus fruit with thick rind and mild sweet segments; called Chakotra in India.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and tangy, less bitter than grapefruit.
texture: Firm, dry-ish segments that hold shape.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical and tropical citrus climate.
growingTips: Large vigorous tree. Peel the thick pith carefully; segments are great in salads.

name: Sweet Lime (Mosambi)
notes: Indian mosambi, juiced widely across the subcontinent for a mild non-acidic refresher.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet with very low acidity.
texture: Juicy, tender segments.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical citrus belt.
growingTips: Reliable bearer in citrus regions. Best enjoyed freshly juiced; thin skin peels easily.

name: Tangerine
notes: Easy-peel loose-skinned citrus closely related to the mandarin.
tasteDescription: Sweet and tangy with a bright aromatic zest.
texture: Juicy, tender, easily separated segments.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical citrus climate; some frost tolerance.
growingTips: Productive small tree, good for containers. Harvest when fully coloured and slightly soft.

name: Key Lime
notes: Small aromatic lime famous for Key lime pie. More fragrant and tart than Persian lime.
tasteDescription: Intensely tart with a strong floral aroma.
texture: Very juicy with thin skin.
climateConditions: Warm frost-free subtropical; thrives in Florida heat.
growingTips: Thorny small tree that does well in pots. Harvest when fruit yields slightly and turns yellowish.

name: Calamondin
notes: Small ornamental sour-citrus prolific in containers; used in marmalades and Filipino cooking.
tasteDescription: Sharply sour with a sweet edible rind.
texture: Juicy with thin tender skin.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical; one of the most cold-tolerant tropical citrus.
growingTips: Heavy continuous bearer, excellent patio tree. Use whole fruit including rind for drinks and preserves.

name: Finger Lime
notes: Australian native producing cylindrical fruit filled with caviar-like juice pearls.
tasteDescription: Tart and zesty with a burst of citrus 'pearls'.
texture: Crisp vesicles that pop like caviar.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical; tolerates partial shade.
growingTips: Thorny slow-growing shrub. Harvest when fruit detaches easily; squeeze out the pearls as garnish.

name: Cashew
notes: Tropical tree producing the cashew nut beneath a fleshy cashew apple, both used in India.
tasteDescription: Nut is rich and buttery; apple is sweet-astringent.
texture: Crunchy nut; soft fibrous apple.
climateConditions: Hot humid coastal tropics; drought tolerant once established.
growingTips: Roast nuts carefully — raw shells contain caustic oil. Apple is juiced or fermented (feni).

name: Pistachio
notes: Desert-adapted nut tree producing green kernels in split shells.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet, buttery and rich.
texture: Crunchy firm kernel.
climateConditions: Hot dry summers and cool winters; very drought and heat tolerant.
growingTips: Needs long hot summers and winter chill, plus a male tree for pollination. Alternate bearing is common.

name: Pecan
notes: Large hickory-family nut tree widely grown across the American South including parts of Florida.
tasteDescription: Rich, buttery and sweet.
texture: Crisp, oily kernel.
climateConditions: Warm humid summers with adequate winter chill.
growingTips: Large long-lived tree needing space and a second variety for pollination. Harvest after husks split.

name: Macadamia
notes: Australian native producing rich buttery nuts in very hard shells.
tasteDescription: Buttery, sweet and delicate.
texture: Crisp yet creamy kernel.
climateConditions: Warm subtropical with reliable moisture.
growingTips: Evergreen tree slow to bear (5–7 years). Collect fallen nuts and cure before cracking.

name: Indian Almond (Badam Tree)
notes: Tropical 'badam' tree (distinct from true almond) with edible almond-flavoured seeds.
tasteDescription: Seed kernel is mildly sweet and almond-like.
texture: Firm crunchy kernel inside a fibrous husk.
climateConditions: Warm coastal tropics; salt and wind tolerant.
growingTips: Large shade tree often planted along avenues and beaches. Crack the hard husk for the small kernel.

name: Coconut
notes: Iconic tropical palm providing water, flesh and oil; central to coastal Indian life.
tasteDescription: Sweet refreshing water; rich nutty flesh.
texture: Soft jelly when young, firm and crunchy when mature.
climateConditions: Hot humid coastal tropics; salt tolerant.
growingTips: Plant in sandy well-drained soil near coasts. Harvest young for water, mature for copra and oil.

name: Date Palm
notes: Desert palm producing sweet dates; grown in arid regions and parts of South Asia.
tasteDescription: Intensely sweet with caramel and honey notes.
texture: Soft and chewy to firm, depending on stage.
climateConditions: Hot arid climate with low humidity at fruiting.
growingTips: Needs intense dry heat to ripen fruit. Requires male and female palms or hand pollination.
healthBenefits: Rich in natural sugars and energy

name: Jackfruit (Kathal - young)
notes: Tender young jackfruit (kathal) used as a meaty vegetable in Indian curries and biryani.
tasteDescription: Neutral and savoury when young; absorbs spices well.
texture: Firm, meaty and fibrous when young.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics; needs space for the very large tree.
growingTips: Harvest small green fruit for cooking, or let mature for sweet ripe pods. Latex-heavy — oil hands when cutting.

name: Breadfruit
notes: Starchy relative of jackfruit cooked like a potato across the tropics.
tasteDescription: Mild and starchy, bread- or potato-like when cooked.
texture: Dense and starchy; creamy when ripe.
climateConditions: Hot humid lowland tropics.
growingTips: Large handsome tree. Harvest mature-green for cooking; roast, boil or fry the flesh.

name: Tamarillo (Tree Tomato)
notes: Egg-shaped tree tomato with tangy flesh used in both sweet and savoury dishes.
tasteDescription: Tangy and tomato-like with sweet-tart fruity notes.
texture: Smooth firm flesh with edible seeds.
climateConditions: Cool subtropical and highland tropics; protect from frost.
growingTips: Fast-growing short-lived shrub-tree bearing in 1–2 years. Peel the bitter skin before eating.

name: White Sapote
notes: Soft cream-fleshed fruit with a custard-like sweetness, related to citrus.
tasteDescription: Sweet with banana, peach and vanilla notes.
texture: Soft, smooth, custardy flesh.
climateConditions: Mild subtropical; more cold tolerant than most tropical fruits.
growingTips: Vigorous tree; thin fruit to improve size. Harvest mature-firm and ripen until it yields to a gentle squeeze.

name: Cricket Ball Sapota
notes: Large round Indian sapota cultivar with abundant sweet malty flesh.
tasteDescription: Sweet with malt, brown-sugar and pear notes.
texture: Soft, grainy, melting flesh.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics; drought tolerant once established.
growingTips: Hardy reliable cropper. Harvest mature fruit and ripen until soft; scrape skin to test for brown flesh.

name: Anjeer (Indian Fig)
notes: Indian fig cultivar (anjeer) grown in Maharashtra and Gujarat, eaten fresh and dried.
tasteDescription: Richly sweet with honeyed jammy notes.
texture: Soft and seedy with a tender skin.
climateConditions: Hot dry subtropical with mild winters.
growingTips: Tolerates heat and poor soil. Harvest when fruit droops and softens; dries excellently in sun.

name: Bhagwa Pomegranate
notes: Premium Indian pomegranate cultivar with glossy red arils and soft seeds, a major export.
tasteDescription: Sweet with a mild tang and very low bitterness.
texture: Juicy crisp arils with soft seeds.
climateConditions: Hot semi-arid; tolerates drought and high heat.
growingTips: Drought-hardy shrub-tree. Withhold water before harvest to concentrate sweetness; protect from fruit cracking.

name: Star Gooseberry (Chalmeri)
notes: Tart pale-green ribbed berries borne in clusters on the trunk, used for pickles and preserves.
tasteDescription: Very sour and crisp.
texture: Hard, crunchy and juicy.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics.
growingTips: Small tree fruiting heavily along its branches. Use in pickles, candies and chutneys.

name: Rose Apple (Gulab Jamun fruit)
notes: Crisp pale fruit with a distinct rosewater aroma, eaten fresh in India and Southeast Asia.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet with a floral rosewater fragrance.
texture: Crisp and watery, like a light apple.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics; needs steady moisture.
growingTips: Attractive small tree. Eat fresh soon after harvest as it does not store well.

name: Water Apple (Jamrul)
notes: Bell-shaped crunchy watery fruit (jamrul) popular in Bengal and Southeast Asia.
tasteDescription: Very mild, lightly sweet and refreshing.
texture: Crisp, spongy and extremely watery.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics with high rainfall.
growingTips: Productive small tree. Eat immediately as fruit bruises and spoils quickly.

name: Indian Persimmon (Amlok/Tendu)
notes: Wild Indian persimmon (tendu) with sweet yellow fruit; its leaves wrap beedis.
tasteDescription: Sweet and mildly astringent when fully ripe.
texture: Soft, pulpy when ripe.
climateConditions: Tropical dry deciduous forests; very hardy.
growingTips: Hardy forest tree. Let fruit fully ripen and soften to remove astringency before eating.

name: Governor's Plum (Ramphal/Lukum)
notes: Small reddish-purple tart-sweet wild fruit common across India, eaten fresh or preserved.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart and slightly astringent.
texture: Juicy with several small seeds.
climateConditions: Tropical and semi-arid; very hardy and drought tolerant.
growingTips: Thorny hardy shrub-tree useful as a hedge. Harvest dark purple fruit; roll between palms to reduce astringency.

name: Monkey Jack (Barhal/Lakoocha)
notes: Jackfruit relative (barhal) with tangy-sweet yellow fruit eaten fresh or pickled in India.
tasteDescription: Sweet-sour and tangy.
texture: Soft fibrous pulp.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics and subtropics.
growingTips: Large handsome tree. Harvest ripe yellow fruit; raw fruit is pickled or cooked.

name: Ramphal (Bullock's Heart)
notes: Large heart-shaped custard-apple relative with smooth reddish skin and sweet pulp.
tasteDescription: Sweet and mild, less fragrant than sitaphal.
texture: Soft, slightly grainy custardy pulp.
climateConditions: Tropical and semi-arid; drought tolerant.
growingTips: Small hardy tree. Harvest mature fruit and ripen until soft; pulp is great in milkshakes.

name: Wild Jamun (Kala Jam)
notes: Smaller wild form of jamun with intensely coloured astringent-sweet berries.
tasteDescription: Tart-sweet and astringent.
texture: Juicy with a large seed.
climateConditions: Tropical and subtropical plains.
growingTips: Hardy tree often found wild. Soak fruit in salt water to reduce astringency before eating.

name: Muskmelon (Kharbooja)
notes: Fragrant netted summer melon (kharbooja) widely grown across northern India.
tasteDescription: Sweet and musky with a floral aroma.
texture: Soft, juicy, melting orange flesh.
climateConditions: Hot dry summers; grown as a warm-season annual vine.
growingTips: Sow after frost in warm soil. Harvest when stem slips easily and aroma is strong.

name: Elephant Apple (Chalta)
notes: Large green fruit (chalta) with tangy pulp used in Bengali and Assamese chutneys and dals.
tasteDescription: Sour and astringent, used mainly in cooking.
texture: Firm fibrous pulp within tough sepals.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics of eastern India.
growingTips: Handsome evergreen with large white flowers. Use the gelatinous pulp for chutneys and curries.

name: Charoli (Chironji)
notes: Source of chironji nuts, small almond-flavoured seeds prized in Indian sweets.
tasteDescription: Nutty and mildly sweet, almond-like.
texture: Soft crunchy seed.
climateConditions: Tropical dry deciduous forests; drought hardy.
growingTips: Slow-growing forest tree. Collect and dry the small seeds; used in kheer, halwa and barfi.

name: Lasoda (Indian Cherry/Gunda)
notes: Sticky-pulped small fruit (gunda) pickled while green across western India.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and mucilaginous when ripe; used green for pickles.
texture: Sticky gummy pulp around a seed.
climateConditions: Hot semi-arid and tropical plains; drought tolerant.
growingTips: Hardy tree giving useful shade. Harvest green for pickling or let ripen for fresh eating.

name: Strawberry Tree (Kaphal)
notes: Himalayan kaphal with small red sweet-tart berries cherished in hill regions.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart and juicy.
texture: Soft and juicy with a single seed.
climateConditions: Cool subtropical Himalayan mid-hills.
growingTips: Hardy hill tree. Harvest fully red ripe berries; eat fresh with a sprinkle of salt as locals do.

name: Yellow Passion Fruit
notes: Vigorous yellow-skinned passion fruit vine well suited to tropical heat.
tasteDescription: Tart and intensely aromatic with tropical floral notes.
texture: Juicy aromatic pulp with crunchy edible seeds.
climateConditions: Warm frost-free tropics and subtropics.
growingTips: Fast-growing vine needing a strong trellis. Harvest fruit after it drops and wrinkles for peak sweetness.

name: Dragon Fruit (Pitaya)
notes: Climbing cactus producing striking pink fruit with speckled flesh; increasingly grown in India.
tasteDescription: Mildly sweet and refreshing, like a light melon-kiwi.
texture: Soft juicy flesh with tiny crunchy seeds.
climateConditions: Hot dry to humid tropics; drought tolerant cactus.
growingTips: Needs a sturdy post or trellis to climb. Hand-pollinate night flowers for reliable fruit set.

name: Prickly Pear (Nagphani)
notes: Cactus fruit (nagphani/thohar) eaten across arid India; sweet magenta pulp full of seeds.
tasteDescription: Sweet and mild, like watermelon with a hint of bubblegum.
texture: Juicy soft pulp with many hard seeds.
climateConditions: Hot arid and semi-arid; extremely drought tolerant.
growingTips: Handle with thick gloves to avoid tiny glochid spines. Singe or peel skin before eating.

name: Indian Olive (Jalpai)
notes: Tart green fruit (jalpai) of eastern India used for pickles, chutneys and tenga dishes.
tasteDescription: Sharply sour and astringent.
texture: Firm fibrous flesh around a hard seed.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics of eastern India.
growingTips: Large evergreen shade tree. Harvest green and use promptly for pickles and souring curries.

name: Santol (Cotton Fruit)
notes: Round fuzzy-skinned fruit with cottony sweet-sour pulp around large seeds.
tasteDescription: Sweet-tart and tangy.
texture: Soft cottony pulp clinging to seeds.
climateConditions: Hot humid lowland tropics.
growingTips: Large productive tree. Suck the pulp from around the seeds; rind can be candied.

name: Salak (Snake Fruit)
notes: Palm fruit with snakeskin-patterned scaly skin and crunchy sweet-tart segments.
tasteDescription: Sweet and tangy with a hint of pineapple and banana.
texture: Crisp and dry, apple-like.
climateConditions: Hot humid equatorial tropics.
growingTips: Spiny clumping palm. Peel the scaly skin like an egg; segments contain a hard seed.

name: Ceylon Olive (Veralu)
notes: Tart green olive-like fruit popular in South Indian and Sri Lankan pickles.
tasteDescription: Sour and astringent, mellowing when pickled.
texture: Crisp firm flesh around a ridged seed.
climateConditions: Warm humid tropics of South India and Sri Lanka.
growingTips: Attractive evergreen. Crush lightly and pickle with salt and chilli, or eat with spice.
